# Measuring Incrementality {#sec-measuring-incrementality}

Every model in this book so far has been trained on attributed outcomes. An install counts when the MMP credits it to an impression the DSP served, and the conversion models in @sec-gradient-boosted-conversion-models learn to predict exactly that. Attribution is how DSPs are evaluated and how most of them are paid, but it answers a different question from the one advertisers care about most. An advertiser wants to know how many installs would not have happened without the DSP. Some attributed installs come from users who were about to install anyway, organically or through another channel, and the DSP's impression only collected the credit.

This matters more as models get better. When I've written about pretraining deep models on non-attributed data, the step I've recommended alongside every A/B test is an incrementality holdout, because the holdout is what shows whether new signals are finding devices that your ads actually influence, rather than devices that would have installed anyway.[^c23-intent] A model that gets very good at predicting attributed installs can get equally good at finding people who were going to install regardless.

In this chapter, we will define incrementality, show how to measure it inside an auction with ghost bids, using the holdout flag the bidder has logged since @sec-logging-at-bid-time, describe the sources of randomness a DSP can use to learn it, estimate incrementality ratios by segment, and report incremental CPI and ROAS next to attributed results. The measurement mechanics build on the auction experiments in @sec-shadow-mode-canaries-and-ab-tests. Models that predict lift per impression, and pricing on that prediction, come in @sec-uplift-modeling.

[^c23-intent]: Ben Weber, "Pretrained Deep Learning Intent Signals for Mobile DSPs," *Medium*, October 3, 2026.

## Attribution Is Not Causation

An install attributed to the DSP can happen in three ways. The DSP's ad caused it. The user would have installed organically, through a store search, a recommendation, or a chart placement. Or the user would have installed through another paid channel, and the DSP's impression won the last touch. As we saw in @sec-measurement-and-mmps, last-touch attribution credits all three to the DSP.

We split the install probability for an impression into a baseline and an uplift:

$$p_{install}(x) = p_0(x) + u(x), \qquad r(x) = \frac{u(x)}{p_{attr}(x)}$$

Here, $p_0(x)$ is the chance that the device installs without our ad, $u(x)$ is the extra chance that our impression causes, $p_{attr}(x)$ is the attributed install rate that our conversion models already predict, and $r(x)$ is the **incrementality ratio**, the share of attributed installs that are actually new.

A DSP can look excellent on attributed CPI and still have a low $r$. This happens most often when models drift toward users who are about to convert anyway, such as recent searchers, heavy players of similar games, and lapsed users of the advertiser's own app. The better a model gets at its attributed objective, the better it can get at collecting credit for installs it didn't cause.

Incrementality also has two sources, and they're worth separating. **Reach** comes from converting users that other channels don't bid on, bid too little on, or can't reach. **Persuasion** comes from changing the behavior of users that other channels also reach, through a better creative, format, frequency, or timing. Both show up as lift in a holdout test, and the segment analysis later in this chapter helps tell them apart. @tbl-c24b-terms defines the terms we'll use.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Attributed installs | Installs the MMP credits to the DSP |
| Incremental installs | Installs that would not have happened without the DSP |
| Incrementality | Incremental installs divided by attributed installs |
| Displacement | Attributed installs that would have come from organic or other channels |
| iCPI | Spend divided by incremental installs |

: Incrementality terms. {#tbl-c24b-terms}

## Measuring Lift with Ghost Bids

A naive comparison of exposed and unexposed users is badly biased, because the bidder chose the exposed users for being likely to install. A plain holdout of users who never get ads is unbiased but diluted, since most held-out users would never have been targeted. **Ghost bids** solve both problems:[^c23-ghost]

1. Assign each user to treatment or control with a stable hash of the device ID, for example 90% and 10%. The assignment applies to every campaign for the advertiser for the length of the test.
2. Run the full bid path for every request. Eligibility, prediction, pricing, shading, and the internal auction are identical for both groups.
3. For treatment users, submit the bid as usual. For control users, log a ghost bid with the would-be bid and its predicted win rate, and send nothing to the exchange.
4. Collect outcomes for both groups from the advertiser's complete install data, including organic and other-channel installs. Control users can never be attributed to the DSP, so attributed data alone can't be used.

![The ghost-bid design. Every request runs through the full bid path. Treatment users get real bids, and control users get a logged ghost bid that is never sent. Lift is the difference in all installs between the two groups, using the advertiser's complete install data.](../images/incr-ghost-bids.png){#fig-c24b-ghost width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of the ghost-bid experiment. Bid requests are split by device hash: 90% treatment users go through the full bid path and get real bids, and 10% control users go through the same path but only a ghost bid is logged. Installs from the MMP are compared between groups."}

The cost of the test is only the impressions withheld from the control group, as shown in @fig-c24b-ghost. No media is spent on control users, which is the main advantage over older designs that served public service ads to a control group. Large-scale field experiments have also shown how far observational comparisons can be from randomized ones in advertising, which is a good reason to insist on randomization.[^c23-gordon]

[^c23-ghost]: Garrett A. Johnson, Randall A. Lewis, and Elmar I. Nubbemeyer, "Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness," *Journal of Marketing Research*, 2017.
[^c23-gordon]: Brett R. Gordon, Florian Zettelmeyer, Neha Bhargava, and Dan Chapsky, "A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook," *Marketing Science*, 2019.

### The Lift Equations

A ghost bid tells us that we would have bid, not that we would have won. So we compare all users who received at least one real or ghost bid, which is an **intent-to-treat** (ITT) comparison, and then correct for the share of treated users who actually saw an ad:

$$\text{ITT} = \bar{Y}_{T,\,bid} - \bar{Y}_{C,\,ghost}, \qquad \pi = P(\text{at least one won impression} \mid T, \text{bid})$$

$$\text{lift per exposed user} = \frac{\text{ITT}}{\pi}, \qquad \text{incremental installs} = \frac{\text{ITT}}{\pi} \times N_{exposed}$$

$$\text{iCPI} = \frac{\text{spend}}{\text{incremental installs}}, \qquad \text{incrementality} = \frac{\text{incremental installs}}{\text{attributed installs}}$$

Here, $\bar{Y}$ is the outcome rate in each group, such as installs, first purchases, or D7 revenue per user. Dividing by $\pi$ is the standard instrumental variables correction, with random assignment as the instrument and exposure as the treatment.

Let's make this concrete. Treated users who received bids install at 0.60%, and control users who received ghost bids install at 0.50%, so the ITT is 0.10 percentage points. If 40% of treated users won at least one impression, the lift per exposed user is $0.10 / 0.40 = 0.25$ points. If the DSP's attributed install rate on exposed users was 0.60%, incrementality is $0.25 / 0.60 \approx 42\%$. More than half of the attributed installs would have happened anyway, and the incremental CPI is about 2.4 times the attributed CPI.

## Displacement by Channel

When the advertiser shares the attributed channel for every install, the difference between groups splits into what the DSP added and what it displaced. @tbl-c24b-displacement shows an example per 100,000 bid-on users, assuming every treated user was exposed, for simplicity.

| Install source | Control (ghost bids) | Treatment (real bids) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Our DSP | 0 | 250 | +250 |
| Largest other network | 300 | 210 | −90 |
| Other paid channels | 100 | 80 | −20 |
| Organic | 200 | 160 | −40 |
| Total | 600 | 700 | +100 |

: Installs by source in a ghost-bid test. {#tbl-c24b-displacement}

$$\text{displacement}_c = -\Delta_c, \qquad \sum_c \text{displacement}_c = \text{attributed} - \Delta_{total}$$

The DSP is credited with 250 installs, but total installs rose by 100, so incrementality is 40%. The other 150 installs were displaced, mostly from another network, as shown in @fig-c24b-displacement. For the advertiser, those installs were paid for twice. For the DSP, the displacement shows which segments overlap with other channels, which is where to look next.

![Installs per 100,000 bid-on users by source, for the control and treatment groups. The DSP is credited with 250 installs, but total installs rise by only 100. The difference comes from installs displaced from another network, other paid channels, and organic installs.](../images/incr-displacement.png){#fig-c24b-displacement width="90%" fig-alt="Stacked bars of installs per 100,000 users. Control totals 600 and treatment totals 700, so the DSP added 100 incremental installs, even though it is credited with 250, because it displaced installs from organic and other channels."}

### Inputs and Practical Limits

| Input | Source |
|---|---|
| User hash and test assignment | Bidder, at request time |
| Test ID, ghost flag, would-be bid, predicted win rate | Bid ledger |
| Exposure (won and billed impressions per user) | Win and billing notices |
| All installs and events for the advertiser's app, with attributed channel | Advertiser's MMP raw data, including organic |
| Spend | Spend accounting |

: Inputs to a ghost-bid test. {#tbl-c24b-inputs}

**Sample size.** Installs are rare, and lift is a small difference between two rates. For a baseline install rate of 0.5% among bid-on users and a 10% relative lift, detecting the difference with 95% confidence and 80% power takes about 312,000 users per group, with an even split and full exposure:

$$n \approx \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,p(1-p)}{\Delta^2}$$

With 40% exposure, the ITT shrinks to 40% of the lift, and the requirement grows to about 1.95 million users per group. With a 90/10 split, the total is about 10.8 million bid-on users. Report confidence intervals, not point estimates, and plan tests in weeks rather than days.

Other practical limits:

- **Complete install data.** The advertiser has to share complete install data for both groups. This is the most important request to make before a test starts.
- **Fixed assignment.** Assignment has to stay fixed for the length of the test, and across all of the advertiser's campaigns on the DSP.
- **Other channels keep running.** Other channels keep running for control users. That's correct, because incrementality is measured on top of everything else the advertiser does.
- **No device ID, no user-level test.** On iOS without a device identifier, user-level randomization isn't possible. We cover geo and switchback designs in @sec-ios-and-contextual-signals.

## Where Randomness Comes From

Uplift can only be estimated where exposure varies for reasons unrelated to the user. A DSP has three sources of that variation, and two of them come almost for free from systems the book has already built, as shown in @tbl-c24b-randomness.

| Source | What is randomized | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ghost-bid holdouts | Whether the user can be exposed at all | Withheld impressions | The cleanest source |
| Bid exploration | The chance of winning each auction | Small, already budgeted | The exploration multiplier from @sec-win-rate-and-bid-shading is an instrument |
| Near-miss auctions | Winning or losing when the bid is close to the clearing price | None | A natural experiment; needs clearing prices on both wins and losses |

: Sources of randomness for estimating uplift. {#tbl-c24b-randomness}

**Bid exploration as an instrument.** When exploration is on, the media value is multiplied by a random factor before shading, which changes the chance of winning for reasons unrelated to the user. Comparing requests with high and low multipliers gives an estimate of uplift per impression won:

$$\hat{u} = \frac{\bar{Y}_{high} - \bar{Y}_{low}}{\bar{W}_{high} - \bar{W}_{low}}$$

where $\bar{Y}$ is the outcome rate and $\bar{W}$ is the observed win rate in each multiplier bucket. This is a Wald estimator. Because exploration already runs to train the win rate model in @sec-win-rate-and-bid-shading, the DSP gets incrementality data without a separate holdout. The estimate is per impression rather than per user, and it measures the effect of one more impression at the current frequency, which is exactly what pricing needs.

**Near-miss auctions.** Requests where the bid landed just above or just below the clearing price are nearly identical, so comparing their outcomes approximates a randomized experiment. This needs clearing prices on losses as well as wins, which only some exchanges report, so it works best as a check on the other two sources.

## Incrementality Ratios by Segment

The simplest approach estimates $r$ per segment from holdouts or exploration, shrinks small segments toward the overall average, and multiplies it into the value. A segment might be an exchange, a user type (new, lapsed, payer), and a frequency bucket:

$$\tilde{r}_s = \frac{n_s\,\hat{r}_s + k\,\bar{r}}{n_s + k}$$

Here, $\hat{r}_s$ is the measured ratio in segment $s$, $n_s$ is the number of incremental installs behind it, $\bar{r}$ is the overall ratio, and $k$ sets the strength of the shrinkage. Segment ratios are coarse, but they're robust with little data, easy to explain to advertisers, and they surface the main patterns quickly. This is where I would start.

## Sizing and Paying for the Holdout

The holdout from @sec-logging-at-bid-time has been running since the first bid: a fixed share of devices, such as 5%, assigned by a hash with its own salt, for whom the bidder computes and logs a bid and doesn't send it. In walk, it becomes a product, not a one-off test, and that raises three questions.

**What does it cost, and who pays?** The holdout's cost is the installs the DSP doesn't deliver to control devices. With a 5% holdout, it's roughly 5% of the DSP's potential volume, a little less in practice, because some of those devices would have been reached on other requests. Someone absorbs that cost. The DSP can absorb it out of its margin, as the price of being able to prove its value. It can share it with advertisers who want the measurement, by agreeing on a holdout as part of the campaign. Or advertisers can opt in to a larger holdout for a defined test period. What matters is deciding up front, and writing it into the contract, because a holdout that an advertiser discovers on their own looks like lost delivery.

**How big does it need to be?** The sample size calculation above shows the problem: installs are rare and lift is a small difference between rates, so a holdout that's adequate for the DSP's total traffic can be far too small for one advertiser. A 5% holdout across the whole platform measures platform-wide incrementality well within weeks. For an individual advertiser, the holdout has to be large enough at that advertiser's volume to detect the lift it cares about, which for small advertisers can mean a much larger share, a much longer window, or pooling with similar advertisers and reporting a shared ratio.

**How is it kept clean?** Assignment stays fixed for the life of the holdout, across all of the advertiser's campaigns, and the holdout's salt is never used by any other experiment. Devices that reset their advertising ID leave the holdout and come back as new devices, which is one source of the contamination discussed in the pitfalls below.

## Reporting Incremental CPI and ROAS

The point of measuring incrementality is to report it, next to the attributed results advertisers already see. For each campaign and period, the report shows:

- **Attributed installs and CPI,** as the MMP reports them.
- **Incremental installs and incremental CPI,** from the holdout, with a confidence interval: spend divided by the installs the DSP caused.
- **The incrementality ratio,** incremental installs divided by attributed installs, which is the single number that explains the gap.
- **Incremental ROAS,** where revenue data is shared, on the same basis.

The worked bid in @sec-inside-a-demand-side-platform showed why this matters. A campaign with an attributed D7 ROAS of 51%, comfortably above its 40% target, had an incremental ROAS of about 34% once a third of its installs turned out to be ones that would have happened anyway.

The gap needs explaining, because an advertiser seeing it for the first time may conclude the DSP is overstating its results. A few points help. Every channel's attributed results include installs that would have happened anyway, so the question is how large each channel's gap is, not whether it has one. The ratio varies by segment, and the segments with the highest ratios, such as users other channels don't reach, are where the DSP adds the most. And the measurement is the same one advertisers would run themselves with a holdout test, built into the platform. Reporting the incremental number, with its uncertainty, is what lets a DSP make the case from Part I: that it causes installs, not just collects credit for them.

## How the Industry Approaches Incrementality Today

Most large platforms optimize on attributed outcomes and leave incrementality to measurement. Meta is the main public exception. It introduced an incremental attribution setting that optimizes delivery for conversions its models predict were caused by an ad, as an alternative to its standard attribution, and has expanded it since its initial launch in 2025.[^c23-meta] Other platforms have partnered with independent measurement firms, so that advertisers can run lift tests on their campaigns. Explicit uplift-based bidding is still the frontier, for three reasons: uplift labels are rare and noisy, holdouts cost revenue, and advertisers' dashboards and MMPs report attributed outcomes.

For a smaller DSP, this is an opportunity. A DSP that measures lift with ghost bids, reports displacement honestly, and offers an incremental goal has something to sell that scale alone doesn't provide.

[^c23-meta]: "Meta Updates Information on Incremental Attribution Conversion Tracking," *Social Media Today*, <https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/meta-updates-information-incremental-attribution-conversion-tracking/>

## First-Time Pitfalls

- **Holdout contamination.** Device ID resets, limited ad tracking, and installs through other paths put holdout devices in front of ads anyway, and move treated devices into the control. Measure exposure in the holdout as well as the treated group, and treat the result as intent to treat, as in the lift equations above.
- **Comparing against the wrong control.** Ghost bids compare devices the DSP would have bid on. Comparing treated devices with all devices in the holdout, including ones the DSP would never have bid on, mixes targeting with lift.
- **Reading results too early.** Installs, and especially revenue, arrive over days. Read the holdout on matured labels only, like every other delayed metric.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it on the simulator"}
Run ghost bids on a 5% device holdout for a simulated month. Estimate the lift, the incrementality ratio, and incremental CPI by campaign, with confidence intervals, and compare them with the true lift from the ground truth. Then shrink the holdout for one small advertiser, and see how wide its interval becomes.

## Conclusion

In this chapter, we measured what the DSP causes. Attribution counts installs the DSP was credited with, and some of them would have happened anyway. Ghost bids on a fixed device holdout measure the lift directly, with intent-to-treat and exposure-adjusted estimates, and displacement separates installs moved from other channels from installs created. Bid exploration and near-miss auctions add sources of randomness, and segment ratios with shrinkage give robust estimates with little data. We sized the holdout per advertiser, decided who pays for it, and reported incremental CPI and ROAS next to attributed results.

The competitive DSP now has all its pieces. What remains is operating it: monitoring, parity, the fallback ladder, on-call, playbooks, and root-cause analysis, now that real goals and real budgets are at stake.
